messages.text: Look, I've run the numbers and the new market rate for this unit is $2,400 a month, so that's where we need to be going forward. I know it's higher than what you're paying now, but my costs have gone up and that's what comparable units are renting for in this area.

*shifts uncomfortably* 

Wow, $2,400? That's... that's a lot more than the $1,800 I'm paying now. I mean, I knew rents were going up, but a $600 increase feels pretty steep. Can you walk me through what you're basing that number on exactly?

Yeah, look, I get it stings a bit, but the market's changed a lot in two years. I've got comps showing units like yours going for $2,350 to $2,450 right now, so $2,400 is actually on the reasonable side of things.

*nods nervously*

Okay, I hear you on the market... but I've been a great tenant, right? Like, I've never been late on rent, no complaints, kept the place in good condition. Doesn't that count for something? What if we met somewhere in the middle — maybe around $2,100 or $2,150?

I appreciate that you've been reliable, I really do — that's why I'm even having this conversation with you instead of just listing it. But being a good tenant doesn't change what I need to charge to cover my mortgage, taxes, and maintenance costs.

*wrings hands*

Yeah, yeah, I get that... I mean, I understand you have expenses. It's just — two grand is what I could maybe stretch to, but $2,400 is really hard. What if I signed a longer lease? Like two years instead of one? Would that help you out and maybe get us to a better number?

A longer lease does help me, that's true, but it doesn't change the fact that $2,400 is what the market's asking for right now. If I lock in a lower rate for two years, I'm leaving money on the table that I can't get back.

*sighs, looking defeated*

I mean... I don't want to move, this place is convenient and I like the neighborhood. What if we did $2,250 for the first year and then it goes to market rate in year two? That way you're not locked in at a low rate forever, but I'm not getting priced out either?

Look, I appreciate the creative thinking, but $2,250 is still cutting into what I need. Here's what I can do though — $2,300 flat for a one-year lease, and then we reassess when it comes up for renewal. That's the best I can do while still keeping this pencil out.

*pauses, feeling the pressure*

$2,300... I mean, that's still a pretty big jump from where I am now. Can I think about it for a couple days? I need to actually crunch my own numbers and see if I can make that work with my budget.

I hear you, but I've got other interested people already asking about this unit, so I need an answer fairly quickly — let's say by end of business tomorrow. If you can't make $2,300 work, then we'll have to go our separate ways, but I'd rather keep you if you can find a way.

*feels stomach drop, speaking quickly*

Oh man, okay... I mean, I really don't want to lose the place. Yeah, $2,300 is tight, but I think I can make it work if I trim some things. Can we just do one more thing though — what if you covered the first month or knocked off a month's rent to help me through the transition? That would really help.
I can't eat a month of rent — that's just not happening. You're getting a good deal at $2,300 considering where the market is, so let's call that the final number and we'll draw up the lease.

*takes a deep breath, feeling cornered*

Yeah, okay... I mean, you're right, I don't want to end up homeless looking for a new place. Let's do it — $2,300 a month starting when?

Great, I'm glad we could work this out. The lease starts on the first of next month, so you've got about three weeks to get your finances in order. I'll have my lawyer draft up the new agreement and get it to you by Friday.
